title: A song with a racing heart
work: Nocturne in F♯ major, Op. 15 No. 2
question: How much can the hushed, quick middle change the song that returns?
intro: The F♯-major melody lingers over its ornaments, then the middle begins to hurry under its breath. Chopin asks for twice the motion, doppio movimento, while keeping the opening of that passage sotto voce. Paderewski’s accounts, separated by twenty years, sit beside Liszt’s pupil d’Albert and the younger pianists Faulkner and Prati.

recordings.label: Eugen d’Albert, 1916
recordings.note: Kempff remembered d’Albert making a single A♯ seem to tremble like a human voice.

recordings.label: Ignacy Jan Paderewski, 1917
recordings.note: In his Victor recordings, Paderewski often spreads chords and lets the two hands enter at different moments.

recordings.label: Ignacy Jan Paderewski, 1937
recordings.note: The pianist who defended stolen time returns to the nocturne twenty years after his New York recording.

recordings.label: Luke Faulkner
recordings.note: Faulkner studied piano and composition at Chetham’s, then trained in music for the screen at Edinburgh.

recordings.label: Patrizia Prati, 2015
recordings.note: A pupil of Aldo Ciccolini and András Schiff, Prati recorded this nocturne at Madrid’s Museum of Romanticism.

passages.label: A sustained song
passages.note: The right hand threads little flourishes through a sustained melody; evenly spaced bass notes and chords hold the phrase beneath it.

passages.label: Before the quickening
passages.note: The F♯-minor phrase falls from its high notes, its little runs marked dolcissimo — very sweetly.

passages.label: Twice the motion
passages.note: A dotted tune rides above quick notes in the same hand. The bass leaps beneath it, and the opening is hushed.

passages.label: The middle gathers force
passages.note: The dotted rhythm grows insistent and the piano gathers force, bringing the restless middle to its climax.

passages.label: A breath before the return
passages.note: The repeated figure slows and dies away. A pause leaves space for the opening melody to return.
